3.title: The Lord Is Faithful
3.overview:
Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord will run ahead, and assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them. Then he deals firmly with a problem that has grown since his first letter: some believers, probably excited about Christ’s return, have stopped working and are living off others while meddling in everyone’s business. Paul had worked night and day to support himself as an example, and had taught them, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.”

The church must withdraw ordinary support and fellowship from such people, so that they are brought to their senses, yet treat them as brothers, not enemies. Those who have carried the load must not grow weary of doing good. The letter ends with peace, Paul’s own signature against forgery, and grace for all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to pray that the Lord’s message will spread and be honoured as it was with them, and that the missionaries will be rescued from wicked people, since not everyone has faith. But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen and protect them from the evil one. Paul is confident they are doing what he commands, and prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faithless, and Faithful

‘Not all have faith’ — ‘but the Lord is faithful’ (vv.2–3): Paul answers human faithlessness not with a better estimate of people but with a reliable Lord, who promises not exemption from trouble but to establish and guard his people through it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul wrote from Corinth, where Acts 18 records exactly the ‘wicked and evil men’ of verse 2.

Now: Confidence placed ‘in the Lord about you’ (v.4) survives disappointment, because it never rested on the people themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.

Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians 3 turns from the great events of the end (chapter 2) to the ordinary life of a church waiting for them. It falls into three parts. First, prayer and confidence (vv. 1–5): Paul asks the church to pray that the gospel will run freely and that he will be rescued from hostile men; he assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them from the evil one; and he prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s steadfastness. Second, a problem of discipline (vv. 6–15): some members had stopped working, perhaps excited by talk of the Lord’s return, and were living off others and meddling in their affairs. Paul commands the church to keep away from them, points to his own example of working night and day, repeats the rule he gave when he was with them (whoever will not work should not eat), orders the idle to work quietly and earn their own living, and tells the church to shun the disobedient, not as enemies but as brothers who need warning. Third, the close (vv. 16–18): a prayer for the Lord of peace to give them peace, Paul’s signature in his own hand as a mark against forgeries, and the blessing of grace. The chapter shows that a right hope of Christ’s coming does not make people idle; it makes them faithful, busy and orderly.

Setting and background. In 1 Thessalonians Paul had already told the church to work with their hands and live quietly (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12) and to warn the idle (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The problem had grown. The false report that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2) may have fed it: if the end is here, why go on working? Or the idle may simply have been taking advantage of the generosity of richer believers, as clients in Greek cities lived off patrons. Either way, Paul treats it as a matter of obedience to the apostolic tradition, not merely of manners.

Finally, brothers, pray for us. Key words. “Finally” (to loipon, as for the rest) marks the move to the closing section, not the very last word. “Pray” is present tense: keep praying. The apostle who prays for them (1:11) asks them to pray for him. Prayer runs both ways in the body of Christ; no minister is above needing the prayers of his people.

That the word of the Lord may speed ahead. Key words. “Speed ahead” (trechō, run) pictures the gospel as a runner racing forward without obstruction, echoing Psalm 147:15, where God’s word runs swiftly. Paul’s first request is not for his own comfort but for the progress of the message. The word is “of the Lord”: it is Christ’s word, carried by Paul.

And be honored, as happened among you. Key words. “Be honored” (doxazō, be glorified). The word is glorified when people receive it as God’s word and their lives are changed by it, as the Thessalonians had received it (1 Thessalonians 1:5–6; 2:13). Their own conversion is the pattern of what Paul prays for elsewhere; at this time he was in Corinth.

And that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. Key words. “Delivered” (rhyomai, rescued). “Wicked” (atopos, literally out of place, perverse, unreasonable) and “evil” (ponēros, actively malicious). The definite article in Greek (“the wicked and evil men”) suggests particular opponents, probably those in Corinth who opposed Paul (Acts 18:5–17). The gospel advances in the face of opposition, and Paul asks for prayer for protection so that the work can continue.

For not all have faith. Key words. Literally, “for not of all is the faith.” This is a sober realism: not everyone believes, and some who reject the gospel actively fight it. It also prepares for verse 3 by contrast: people are unfaithful, but the Lord is faithful. Unbelief is the root of opposition to the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the progress of the gospel depends finally on our prayers rather than on God. God has ordained that his purposes advance through the prayers of his people; prayer is a real means he uses, not a lever that overrules him. Nor does “not all have faith” mean that faith is something all people could produce if only they tried harder; faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29), which is why Paul prays.

In a sentence. Last of all, keep praying for us: that the Lord’s message will race on and be honoured everywhere as it was with you, and that we will be rescued from perverse and malicious men, because faith is not something everyone has.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week for one missionary or minister by name: that the word would run through their work, and that they would be protected from those who oppose it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.

But the Lord is faithful. Key words. A deliberate play on words in Greek: “not all have faith (pistis)” (v. 2), “but faithful (pistos) is the Lord.” Human faithlessness is set against the Lord’s faithfulness. The word stands first in the Greek sentence for emphasis. “The Lord” here is Christ, as throughout these letters. His faithfulness means he keeps his promises and finishes what he begins (1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9; Philippians 1:6).

He will establish you. Key words. “Establish” (stērizō, make firm, set fast, strengthen). The same word as in 2:17 and 1 Thessalonians 3:2, 13. Paul turns quickly from his own danger to theirs. They were under persecution; the Lord himself would hold them up.

And guard you against the evil one. Key words. “Guard” (phylassō, keep watch over, protect, like a garrison). “The evil one” (tou ponērou) could grammatically mean “evil” in general, but here, after chapter 2’s talk of Satan’s activity (2:9), it almost certainly means Satan himself, as in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13) and Jesus’ prayer for his disciples (John 17:15). Satan wants to shake believers loose, by persecution, by false teaching, or by disorder in the church. Christ guards his own.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer finally fall away? Arminian and some Lutheran traditions teach that a genuine believer may lose salvation by turning away. Verdict: Verses like this one ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance. The promise rests not on our grip on Christ but on his faithfulness: “he will establish you and guard you.” Those whom God has chosen and called (2:13–14) he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; 1 Peter 1:5). This does not make warnings pointless; the warnings are among the means by which he keeps us. And those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never be attacked or never stumble. Satan does attack, and believers do sin. It means the Lord will not let the evil one finally destroy their faith. Nor does it make us passive: Paul still commands them (v. 4) and prays for them (v. 5).

In a sentence. People may be faithless, but the Lord is utterly faithful: he will make you stand firm and keep you safe from Satan.

For worship. When you feel your own grip on faith is weak, rest on his faithfulness. Thank him that your safety depends on his keeping, not on your strength.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.

And we have confidence in the Lord about you. Key words. “Have confidence” (peithō, perfect tense, be persuaded, trust). Paul’s confidence is not in the Thessalonians’ natural goodness but “in the Lord”: because the Lord is at work in them (v. 3), Paul can trust that they will obey. This is a pastoral move before the hard command of verse 6: he expresses trust before giving correction.

That you are doing and will do the things that we command. Key words. “Command” (parangellō, give orders, charge, a military and legal word). It appears four times in this chapter (vv. 4, 6, 10, 12). Paul speaks with apostolic authority: his instructions are not suggestions but the Lord’s commands through his apostle (1 Thessalonians 4:2). The church is already obeying and will go on obeying.

May the Lord direct your hearts. Key words. “Direct” (kateuthynō, make straight, guide straight along a path), the same verb as in 1 Thessalonians 3:11. Obedience is not merely outward; it begins in the heart, and only the Lord can steer the heart (Proverbs 21:1).

To the love of God. Key words. Grammatically this could be our love for God or God’s love for us. Most likely Paul means God’s love for us: may the Lord lead you deeper into the experience and knowledge of God’s love (Romans 5:5; Ephesians 3:19), from which our love for God flows. Both are true, and the first produces the second.

And to the steadfastness of Christ. Key words. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē, patient endurance, bearing up under a load). Again either Christ’s own endurance, which they are to see and share (Hebrews 12:2–3), or the endurance that Christ gives and that waits for him. Probably both: the patient endurance that Christ showed under suffering, which he now works in his people as they wait for his return. This is the right response to chapter 2: not feverish excitement, but steady endurance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s authority was his own. He commands “in the Lord.” Nor does it mean obedience is earned salvation; it is the fruit of hearts that the Lord has directed into his love.

In a sentence. Because the Lord is at work in you, we are sure you are doing, and will keep doing, what we instruct; may he steer your hearts deep into God’s love and into the steady endurance that Christ showed and gives.

For worship. Pray this for yourself today: “Lord, steer my heart into your love, and give me the endurance of Christ.”

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–15 – Idleness, and How to Deal With It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul commands them, in the Lord’s name, to keep away from any believer who lives in idleness, refusing to work. The missionaries themselves set the example: they did not eat anyone’s food without paying, but worked hard night and day so as not to burden anyone, not because they had no right to support, but to give a model to copy. Their rule was that anyone unwilling to work should not eat. Some are idle busybodies; they must settle down and earn their own living. The others must not grow tired of doing good. Anyone who ignores this letter is to be noted and avoided, so that he is ashamed, yet treated as a brother to be warned, not as an enemy.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discipline That Aims at Restoration

Verses 14 and 15 must be held together: the withdrawal is real, and its aim is the offender's own recovery; and he is still to be warned as a brother. Drop the firmness and the church helps nobody; drop the warmth and discipline becomes expulsion.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul could command the idle to work only because he had worked night and day in front of them, declining support he had every right to (vv.7–9).

Now: Verse 10 is about the unwilling, not the unable, and it governs the church's own table. And verse 13 speaks to the faithful who have carried more than their share: do not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.

Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The fullest and most solemn form of authority Paul could use: not his own name, but Christ’s. “In the name of” means by his authority and as his representative. What follows is not advice but a binding instruction for the church.

That you keep away from any brother. Key words. “Keep away” (stellesthai, draw back, hold aloof, withdraw from). The word was used of furling sails or keeping one’s distance. The person is still called a “brother”: this is discipline inside the family of faith, not a declaration that he is an unbeliever. The point is to stop treating him as though nothing were wrong, so that he feels the weight of the church’s disapproval.

Who is walking in idleness. Key words. “In idleness” (ataktōs, disorderly, out of line). The word was used of soldiers breaking ranks, and in everyday papyri of apprentices skipping work. In context (vv. 7–12) the specific disorder is refusing to work and living off others. “Walking” is the Bible’s word for a settled way of life, not a single slip.

And not in accord with the tradition that you received from us. Key words. “Tradition” (paradosis, what is handed down), the same word as in 2:15. The apostolic tradition included not only doctrine but how to live, including the duty to work (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12). This tradition is now found in the New Testament, the written form of what the apostles handed down.

Setting and background. Why might some have stopped working? Three main suggestions: (1) eschatological excitement, believing the day had come (2:2) and that work was pointless; (2) a culture of patronage, in which poorer people attached themselves to wealthier ones and lived on handouts, now transferred to generous church members; (3) a misunderstanding of Christian love, assuming the church owed them support. Paul’s answer covers all three: work is part of faithful waiting, love does not mean being a burden, and the church must not enable idleness.

Where Christians differ: how should church discipline be practised? Some churches practise almost no formal discipline; others make it harsh and quick. Verdict: Scripture requires real discipline, carried out by the church under its elders, aimed at restoring the sinner (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1). This passage describes a step short of full exclusion: the person is still a brother (v. 15), but the church withdraws close fellowship to bring him to shame and repentance. Discipline is graded to the offence and persistence, and it is always done in love, never as revenge.

What it does not mean. It does not mean shunning those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age, or lack of jobs. The issue is those who will not work (v. 10). Scripture repeatedly commands care for the genuinely needy (Galatians 2:10; 1 Timothy 5:3–16). Nor does it mean cutting off all contact; verse 15 says to warn him, which requires speaking.

In a sentence. By the authority of the Lord Jesus Christ we instruct you to hold yourselves apart from any fellow believer who has broken ranks and lives in idleness, contrary to the teaching we handed on to you.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: does your church’s kindness ever enable someone’s settled refusal to take responsibility? Loving them may mean refusing to go along with it.
verseByVerse.note: The problem of idleness in the church is now worse than when Paul wrote the first letter.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.

For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us. Key words. “Imitate” (mimeomai, follow as an example; our word “mimic”). Paul often calls believers to follow his example as he follows Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1; Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). Doctrine was taught by word and shown by life. “You ought” (dei, it is necessary): this imitation is a duty.

Because we were not idle when we were with you. Key words. “Were not idle” (ouk ētaktēsamen, we did not break ranks), the verb form of the word in verse 6. Paul and his companions did not behave in the disorderly way some were now behaving.

Nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it. Key words. “Eat bread” is a Hebrew way of saying get one’s living (Genesis 3:19; Amos 7:12). “Without paying” (dōrean, as a gift, free). Paul did not live on anyone’s charity while in Thessalonica, though the Philippians sent him gifts there (Philippians 4:16).

But with toil and labor we worked night and day. Key words. “Toil” (kopos, wearying work) and “labor” (mochthos, hardship, hard struggle). The same pair as in 1 Thessalonians 2:9. Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), working with leather, and he worked long hours, probably starting before dawn, while also preaching and teaching.

That we might not be a burden to any of you. Key words. “Be a burden” (epibareō, weigh down). Paul did not want his support to fall on a young, poor and persecuted church, and he did not want anyone to say he preached for money (1 Thessalonians 2:5–6; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9).

It was not because we do not have that right. Key words. “Right” (exousia, authority, entitlement). Paul firmly taught that those who preach the gospel have the right to be supported by it (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18; Luke 10:7). He gave up this right voluntarily.

But to give you in ourselves an example to imitate. Key words. “Example” (typos, pattern, model, the impression left by a stamp). Paul deliberately made himself a living pattern of honest work, so that no one could excuse idleness by appeal to spirituality. If the apostle himself worked, so could they.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should never be paid. Paul defends the right of ministers to support elsewhere, and Scripture commands it. It means ministers may sometimes waive that right for the sake of the gospel, and that all believers, including ministers, should model diligence. Nor does it mean manual work is less spiritual than preaching; Paul did both, and both were service to Christ.

In a sentence. You know well that you should follow our pattern: we did not break ranks while we were with you or live on anyone’s handouts, but worked hard and long, day and night, so as not to weigh on any of you; we had every right to support, but we gave it up to make ourselves a model for you to copy.

On a Tuesday. Do your work today as part of your witness. Someone is watching how a Christian works.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.

For even when we were with you, we would give you this command. Key words. “We would give” is the imperfect tense: we kept giving it, repeatedly. This was not a new rule invented for the crisis but part of Paul’s basic instruction to new converts. Teaching about work was part of discipleship from the beginning.

If anyone is not willing to work. Key words. The key word is “willing” (thelei, wants, chooses). The rule targets those who refuse to work, not those who are unable. Paul is dealing with a choice of the will, not with misfortune.

Let him not eat. Key words. A command (third-person imperative), not merely a prediction. The church was not to feed those who could work but would not. Similar sayings existed in Jewish wisdom (Proverbs 10:4; 19:15; 20:4) and the principle reaches back to creation: humanity was made to work (Genesis 2:15), and after the fall work became toil but remained a calling (Genesis 3:19).

Setting and background. Early churches shared meals and supported the needy generously (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35). That generosity could be exploited. This rule protects the church’s charity for those who truly need it, and protects the idle from the harm of being enabled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean refusing help to the sick, disabled, elderly, unemployed through no fault of their own, or those caring for others. Nor does it mean that a person’s worth depends on productivity; every human bears God’s image. It also does not by itself settle every question of public welfare policy; Paul is speaking to the church about its own members. What it does mean is that able people who refuse to work should not expect others to support them, and that true love sometimes says no.

In a sentence. Even while we were among you we kept giving this rule: whoever refuses to work should not be fed.

On a Tuesday. Work is a gift and a calling from God, not just a way to pay the bills. Do today’s work as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23).

verseByVerse.quote: For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.

For we hear that some among you walk in idleness. Key words. Paul had received a report, perhaps from the bearer of the first letter. “Some” (tinas): not the whole church, but a group. “Walk in idleness” (peripatountas ataktōs), the same word as verse 6: living a disorderly life.

Not busy at work, but busybodies. Key words. A wordplay in Greek: mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous, “not working, but working around,” not busy, but busy in others’ business. The English “busybodies” catches the idea. Idleness is rarely restful; those who do not do their own work tend to meddle in other people’s, spreading gossip, interfering, perhaps stirring up excitement about the end. Idleness and meddling go together (1 Timothy 5:13).

Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Paul speaks directly to the idle. “Command” (parangellō) and “encourage” (parakaleō, urge, exhort, appeal): firm authority with a warm appeal. “In the Lord Jesus Christ”: both the authority and the motive are Christ. Paul does not write them off; he calls them back.

To do their work quietly. Key words. “Quietly” (meta hēsychias, with quietness, calmness). The opposite of the restless, meddling busyness of verse 11. It echoes 1 Thessalonians 4:11: aspire to live quietly, mind your own affairs, and work with your hands. Quietness here is not silence but a settled, undisturbed way of life.

And to earn their own living. Key words. Literally, “that they eat their own bread.” Bread they have earned, not bread given by others (contrast v. 8). Self-support is a mark of Christian maturity, and it frees the person to be generous to others (Ephesians 4:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be in paid employment. Homemaking, caring for family, study and volunteer service are real work. The issue is refusing responsibility and living off others while meddling in their affairs.

In a sentence. We are told that some of you are living disorderly lives, not doing any work but busy poking into other people’s business; to such people we give this instruction and appeal, in the Lord Jesus Christ: settle down, get on with your work, and eat bread you have earned.

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself with energy for others’ business, ask whether your own work is done. Quiet faithfulness is a powerful witness.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: not busy at work (ergazomenous) but busybodies (periergazomenous).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.

As for you, brothers. Key words. “As for you” (hymeis de, but you) turns from the idle to the rest of the church, the faithful majority who were working and perhaps supporting the idle.

Do not grow weary in doing good. Key words. “Grow weary” (enkakeō, lose heart, become discouraged, give up). “Doing good” (kalopoieō, doing what is fine, noble, right), a single compound word. The faithful might be tempted to grow cynical: having been taken advantage of, they might stop helping anyone. Paul says: do not let the misuse of your generosity by a few make you stop doing good to all. Keep working, keep giving to the truly needy, keep acting rightly. The same exhortation appears in Galatians 6:9, with the promise that in due season we will reap if we do not give up.

What it does not mean. It does not contradict verse 10. Refusing to enable idleness is itself doing good. The point is that the church should not swing from naive generosity to cold suspicion.

In a sentence. But you, brothers and sisters, must not lose heart or tire of doing what is right.

On a Tuesday. Has disappointment made you stop helping people? Ask God for wisdom to help well and for grace not to grow weary.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.

If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter. Key words. “What we say in this letter”: Paul’s written word carries the same authority as his spoken word (2:15). Refusing it is refusing apostolic authority. This bears on how we treat the New Testament today: it is the apostles’ word to the church, and it binds us.

Take note of that person. Key words. “Take note” (sēmeioō, mark, signal, identify). The church is to recognise publicly who is persisting in disobedience. Not gossip, but a recognised step of church discipline.

And have nothing to do with him. Key words. “Have nothing to do with” (mē synanamignysthai, do not mix together with, do not associate closely). The same rare word as 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11. It likely means withdrawing table fellowship and close social intimacy, possibly including the Lord’s Supper, so that the person feels the break.

That he may be ashamed. Key words. “Be ashamed” (entrepō, literally turn in on oneself, be made to reflect, feel shame). The aim is not humiliation for its own sake but repentance: shame that leads him to see his sin and return.

Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother. Key words. “Warn” (noutheteō, admonish, literally put in mind, counsel). He is still a brother. The church does not hate him, curse him or treat him as an outsider. It continues to speak to him, lovingly and seriously, calling him back. Discipline is family correction, not the expulsion of an enemy.

Where Christians differ: is this the same as excommunication? Some see this as full exclusion from the church; others as a lesser stage. Verdict: This seems to be a step short of full excommunication. In Matthew 18:17 and 1 Corinthians 5:5, 13, the unrepentant is put outside and treated as an unbeliever. Here the offender is still to be warned “as a brother.” Discipline has stages: private warning, warning with witnesses, the church’s withdrawal of close fellowship, and, if repentance never comes, removal from membership. At every stage the goal is restoration (2 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 6:1).

What it does not mean. It does not license harshness, public shaming for entertainment, or cutting off all contact. Paul explicitly forbids treating him as an enemy. Nor does it mean individuals should begin discipline on their own; it is the church’s act, led by its elders.

In a sentence. If anyone refuses to follow what we have written in this letter, mark him out and keep away from close company with him, so that he is brought to shame and reflection; yet do not treat him as an enemy, but keep admonishing him as a brother.

On a Tuesday. If you must correct a fellow believer, do it as family: seriously, but with love and hope of restoration.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the Lord of peace will give them peace at all times and in every way, and be with them all. He adds a greeting in his own handwriting, the mark of every genuine letter from him, and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord of Peace, and a Signature Against Forgery

Only here does Paul write ‘the Lord of peace’, saying of Christ what a Jew would say of God; and his handwritten signature (v.17) answers the forged letter of 2:2 with a test the church can actually use.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To a year-old, harassed congregation Paul wrote of flaming fire and the son of destruction, and signed off with grace.

Now: ‘All’, twice in three verses (vv.16, 18), puts even the disciplined inside the blessing — the difference between discipline and rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.

Now may the Lord of peace himself. Key words. “The Lord of peace”: Christ, who is the source and giver of peace (John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14). Elsewhere Paul says “the God of peace” (1 Thessalonians 5:23; Romans 15:33); here the title is given to the Lord Jesus, a quiet sign of his deity. “Himself” stresses that peace comes directly from him, not from circumstances.

Give you peace at all times in every way. Key words. “Peace” (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom): not only calm feelings, but wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and one another. This church had persecution from outside (1:4), false teaching about the end (2:2), and disorder within (3:6–12). Christ’s peace reaches into all of it: “at all times” (in every circumstance, constantly) and “in every way” (in every form; some manuscripts read “in every place”).

The Lord be with you all. Key words. The greatest blessing is the Lord’s presence (Matthew 28:20). “You all”: including the idle and those being disciplined. Paul’s blessing does not exclude them.

What it does not mean. It does not promise an absence of trouble. Peace is given in the midst of trouble (John 16:33; Philippians 4:7).

In a sentence. May the Lord who is peace himself give you his peace always and in every circumstance; the Lord be with every one of you.

For worship. Ask the Lord of peace for his peace in the specific trouble you face today, and rest in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.

I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Key words. Paul normally dictated his letters to a secretary (an amanuensis; compare Romans 16:22, where Tertius names himself) and then took the pen for the last lines (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). His handwriting was evidently distinctive (Galatians 6:11, “large letters”).

This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine. Key words. “Sign” (sēmeion, mark, token). Paul emphasises it here because a letter falsely claiming to be from him had confused the church about the day of the Lord (2:2). His handwritten signature lets them tell his true letters from forgeries. “In every letter” implies Paul had already written others, or intended this as his regular practice, and that the church would keep and compare his letters.

It is the way I write. Key words. Literally, “thus I write.” His own hand is the guarantee.

Textual note. Some critical scholars argue that 2 Thessalonians was not written by Paul, partly because of its strong stress on authenticity, claiming a forger would protest too much. But the stress fits the situation exactly: a forged letter had already caused trouble (2:2). The early church received the letter as Paul’s without dispute; it is listed in Marcion’s canon and the Muratorian Fragment, and cited by Polycarp and Irenaeus. There is no good reason to doubt it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the signed lines are inspired. The whole letter carries Paul’s apostolic authority; the signature authenticates all of it.

In a sentence. I, Paul, add this greeting in my own handwriting; it is the mark that proves every letter of mine is genuine, and this is how I sign.

On a Tuesday. God cared that his people could tell true teaching from false. Test what you hear against the genuine apostolic word, the Scriptures.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed off in his own hand — a safeguard against forgeries such as the one hinted at in 2:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Grace” (charis, undeserved favour and its gifts). Paul began with grace (1:2) and ends with grace. Everything in between, comfort in persecution, hope of glory, correction of error, discipline, rests on grace. It is the grace of “our Lord Jesus Christ”: it comes to us from him and through him, the crucified and risen Lord.

Be with you all. Key words. The same as 1 Thessalonians 5:28, but with “all” added, as in verse 16. After the stern words of verses 6–15, Paul pointedly includes everyone. Grace is for the whole church, including the disorderly, whom grace alone can restore.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace ignores sin. The same letter disciplines sin. Grace both forgives and transforms (Titus 2:11–12).

In a sentence. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest on every one of you.

For worship. End today by thanking Christ for his grace: it began your Christian life, it carries you now, and it will bring you home.
